When "upward" is used as an adjective, it means directed toward, moving toward, or tending toward a higher place, level, or position. You place it before a noun to describe that noun as having a quality of rising, climbing, or increasing — of going from a lower point to a higher one.

That is the heart of the word. Everything else flows from this.

In its most concrete sense, "upward" describes something that is physically oriented toward a higher position in space — toward the sky, a ceiling, a mountaintop, or simply somewhere above the current point.

An upward slope is a slope that rises as you walk along it — the ground gets higher with every step. An upward glance means your eyes are directed toward something above you. An upward thrust is a force that pushes something into the air, higher than where it started.

Picture a rocket the moment it launches. The direction it travels, the force that propels it, the path it follows — all of that is upward. The word captures the idea of heading higher.

This is where "upward" becomes especially powerful, because it is used just as commonly — perhaps even more commonly — to describe abstract things that have no physical height at all. In these cases, "higher" means more, better, greater, or more advanced.

An upward trend in prices means prices are steadily increasing over time. An upward revision of an estimate means a number has been adjusted to a higher figure. Upward pressure on something — wages, costs, inflation — means there are forces pushing that thing to rise. An upward trajectory in someone's career means their professional life is advancing, improving, progressing.

The phrase upward mobility is a particularly important and common one. It refers to a person's ability to rise from a lower social or economic class to a higher one — to improve their standing in life, earn more money, or gain more status. It is entirely figurative, yet "upward" feels perfectly natural because we culturally think of success as being "higher" and struggle as being "lower."

In all these figurative uses, "upward" signals the same essential thing: movement or tendency toward something greater.
How to Recognize "Upward" as an Adjective

The adjective form of "upward" sits directly in front of a noun and describes it. This positioning — before the noun — is the clearest signal that it is functioning as an adjective.

Notice the pattern:

  • an upward movement
  • an upward climb
  • an upward spiral
  • upward pressure
  • an upward trend
  • upward mobility

In every case, "upward" tells you something essential about the noun it precedes: that the noun involves or is directed toward a higher point or level.

It helps to contrast this briefly with how "upward" works as an adverb, just so you don't confuse the two. In the sentence "She looked upward," the word "upward" is not describing a noun — it is describing how she looked, modifying the verb. But in "She gave an upward glance," it sits before the noun "glance" and describes it. That is the adjective at work.
Subtle but Important Nuance: Direction vs. State

"Upward" as an adjective almost always implies movement or tendency, not simply a static position. It is not just about being high — it is about going higher or pointing higher. A mountain peak is high, but you would not call it "upward." An arrow aimed at the sky, a rising graph, a career in progress — these are "upward" because they involve motion, direction, or inclination toward something higher.

This is what separates "upward" from simply saying something is "high" or "elevated." Upward carries energy and direction within it.
The One Idea to Carry With You

Whenever you see "upward" placed before a noun, ask yourself one question: Is this noun moving toward, pointing toward, or tending toward a higher point — physically or figuratively? If yes, that is exactly what "upward" is describing. Whether it is a slope rising toward a hilltop, a price rising toward a new high, or a life rising toward greater opportunity, the adjective "upward" captures that quality of going from lower to higher in every sense of the word.
